E1196.summary: The initial nothingness of all things, which Atwood says Parmenides and others were cited to prove, and at which the soul does not stop but passes into true Being.
E1196.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “Parmenides and the rest cited to prove the same initial nonentity of all” [III.2 ¶54]. The soul, she continues, “not enduring any longer to stop at nonentity, becomes into true Being” [III.2 ¶55]. Nonentity is thus apparently a stage the soul passes through, not its goal.

E1197.summary: Author of the verse Ordinal of Alchemy, an authority Atwood cites throughout and endorses on secrecy, the few chosen, patience, purity, learning and the requisites of the work.
E1197.body:
Norton's *Ordinal* is cited throughout the book, almost always in support of Atwood's own positions.

**Secrecy and the few chosen.** From the Proheme Atwood takes the point that masters wrote under coverts, while “Yet Anaxagoras wrote plainest of them all In his boke of Conversions Naturall;” [I.1 ¶14, I.1 n21]. He supports the view that few are chosen and covetousness disqualifies: “Quod inter mille millia, vix subt tres electi” [I.1 ¶40, I.1 n47]; “Scarcely seven men maie this science finde.” — the science being granted to few faithful, lowly men and withheld from proud clerks who then call it fable [III.4 ¶14, III.4 n9]. Secrecy is a duty because “If one evil man had hereof his will, All Christian peace he might easily spill;” [I.3 n15]; the art is a holy gift taught orally under oath to the proven [III.4 ¶9–10, III.4 n8]: “Wherefore old Fathers, conveniently, Called this science Holy Alkimy”.

**Name and profundity.** “For it is most profounde philosophye This subtill science of holy Alkimy” [I.1 ¶49, I.1 n59; cf. I.2 ¶51]. In chap. 1 he also illustrates the universal craze for alchemy, the ruin of hasty seekers and the damage done by a monk's book of false receipts [I.1 ¶49–54].

**Order of the work.** He supports white-before-red: “Till the white medicine be fully wrought;” [I.1 ¶59–64, I.1 n64]; Atwood praises the *Ordinal* as candid and orderly except for the concealed Subject Matter. He notes that the parts are divided among authors: “Every and each of them disclosed but a parte” [I.1 ¶83, I.1 n107]. Verse on the never-wasting Water cites Democrit and Hermes [III.3 ¶73–74, III.3 n48].

**Conditions and practice.** Only those of stable wit finish [III.4 ¶16–17]; the Work begins only after purity: “The philosopher’s worke doe not begin Till all things be pure without and within” [IV.1 ¶49, IV.1 n42]; “Greate neede hath he to be a clerke” [IV.2 ¶5, IV.2 n6]. He is the main authority on vessels, ministers, furnaces and places: “Si Deus non dedisset nobis vas Nihil dedisset, and that is glasse” [III.4 ¶30–41]; Atwood calls his account of the Preparatory Practice naive and “without much envy”. He also supports astrological election and the Elixir as a thing of Second Intention [IV.2 ¶34, IV.2 n23], and advice on servants [IV.1 ¶9].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is cited for the name Holy Alchemy [APP ¶29] and against over-haste: “Haste is the Devil’s part” [APP ¶103].

E1198.summary: Norton's verse treatise, cited in IV.1 as the main verse authority on the conduct and hazards of the Gross Work.
E1198.body: Cited from chap. 4 (as Ordinal or Norton’s Ordinal) as Atwood's main verse authority on balanced, unhasty feeding of the work, its cost, patience and simmering, the three-year Gross Work, and the Gross Work as a foul, perilous handicraft needing experience, uniformity and able ministers [IV.1 ¶12–28, IV.1 n14, n17, n22, n23]: “Excess of one half quarter of an hour May destroy all”. See also Norton.

E1199.summary: In Atwood's usage, that which is before all things, in which the Eternal Will arises and into which Wisdom returns; knowing Nothing means having the All.
E1199.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) writes of “bringing back into the Nothing which is before all things” as Wisdom's end; the Eternal Will arises in it [APP ¶90, Appendix, later layer]. Earlier she says: “For he who in such wise knows Nothing --- no one apostate particular --- has the All” [IV.4 ¶27], so knowing Nothing apparently means holding to no separated particular.

E1200.summary: “Night of body or corporeal sleep”: a name Atwood reports for the Terrestrial Paradise, where souls are dead to this life and more alive in that.
E1200.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) identifies it with the Terrestrial Paradise or Elysium: “the true Terrestrial Paradise, which some have called nox corporis, the night of body or corporeal sleep” [II.4 ¶9]. The text glosses the Latin itself. Souls there are dead to this life and more alive in that [II.4 ¶9].

E1201.summary: Nature's three dimensions as displayed by the Spirit in her emanative Law.
E1201.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) calls number, weight and measure the dimensions the Spirit displays in Nature's emanative Law: “For these are the length, and breadth, and profundity of Nature” [III.3 ¶67].

E1202.summary: Outwardly mere 'bark' of things; theosophically, the order in which the Divine Law develops in creative operation, known through theurgic art.
E1202.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood (ATWOOD) says “Numerical numbers are merely the bark of things” [APP ¶107]; understood theosophically, numbers are the order of development of the Divine Law in creative operation, known through theurgic art [APP ¶107].

E1203.summary: Author cited from Sal, Lumen et Spiritus Mundi and Tractatus de Vero Sale on the mineral spirit, gold's magnetical virtue, and innate heat.
E1203.body: Introduced as “another” authority on the power of the pure mineral spirit, which “it will work such an alteration in things of like nature with themselves, that they shall equalize the Philosophical Elixir” [I.2 ¶49, I.2 n49] (Sal, Lumen et Spiritus Mundi, ed. Combachius). The *Tractatus de Vero Sale* is footnoted as the source for gold's magnetical virtue and the names Microcosmic Sun and Stone of Fire [II.1 n21]. From the Latin of Combachius Atwood takes that the effective heat is innate, a terrestrial sun, not external: “sed potius solis terrestris innatus calor” [IV.1 ¶43, IV.1 n39]. She cites him in support throughout.

E1204.summary: The state of the mental eye when all thought is submerged: a crass, obscure vacuity, called the Original of Life, related to true Being as night to day.
E1204.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) describes the objectless mental eye, all thought submerged, becoming one with darkness as the eye does: “a crass, obscure vacuity” [III.2 ¶54]. She identifies it: “that obscure oblivion which is the Original of Life” [III.2 ¶54]. It stands to true Being as night to day [III.2 ¶54].

E1205.summary: The art Atwood says Alexandrian Christian Platonists and divines studied and discussed; St John is said to have practised it for healing and making gold, silver and gems.
E1205.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) reports the Alexandrian Christian Platonists and divines “studying and discussing the Occult Art in their writings”, and that St John is said to have practised it for healing and for making gold, silver and gems [I.1 ¶24].

E1206.summary: The hidden discovery on which, Atwood says, the systems of ancient philosophy were uniformly based; the passage does not say what it is.
E1206.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) refers to “that occult discovery on which the systems of ancient philosophy appear to have been very uniformly based” [I.1 ¶12], without here naming it.

E1207.summary: The hidden material of the art, to which the adepts claim the Bononian Enigma exclusively refers.
E1207.body: Reported as the adepts' view (QUOTED: the adepts): the Bononian Enigma refers exclusively to “the occult material of their art” [I.1 ¶20].

E1208.summary: Atwood's name for the subject of her inquiry, considered in its means and principles, and for the medieval epoch she surveys.
E1208.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) frames her inquiry around “the means and principles of occult science” [I.1 ¶2] and calls the medieval period “this extraordinary epoch of Occult Science” [I.1 ¶39]. Agrippa received “the means and principles of the Occult Science” from Trithemius, and Ashmole and Boorhaave are said to be acquainted with it [I.1 ¶64].

E1209.summary: The hidden Medicine that the Light of Faith discovers when it searches the interior.
E1209.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) says the Light of Faith, searching the interior, discovers “the occult Stone --- the hidden Medicine” [III.1 ¶36], identifying the two.

E1210.summary: A supposed 'New Imponderable' suggested by recent experiments and Mesmerism, which Atwood says few believe in and does not assume.
E1210.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) mentions “the supposition of a New Imponderable, or Odic Force” [I.2 ¶16], suggested by recent experiments and Mesmerism; few believe in it, and she does not assume it in her argument [I.2 ¶16].

E1211.summary: Mythic figure Atwood uses as an image of the inquirer who solves the Sphinx's riddle by the Light of true Chemistry and by unhasty, rational self-penetration.
E1211.body: Atwood uses Oedipus illustratively. Aided by the Light of true Chemistry, he vanquishes the Metaphysical Monster and enters the Temple of Truth [III.1 ¶4]. His lameness signifies not hastening to solve the Sphinx's riddle [IV.1 ¶13]. The one who rationally penetrates his own natural understanding, “like Oedipus, is able to solve the Enigma of the Sphinx” [IV.1 ¶48].

E1212.summary: In a passage given as Hermes', the second of the three that come from two, holding a blackness that must be removed.
E1212.body: Voice: QUOTED: Hermes. The oily tincture is second of the three produced from two: “then the oily tincture” [I.3 ¶23]; it holds a blackness to be removed [I.3 ¶23].

E1213.summary: 'The learned Dane', author of De Ortu et Progressu Chemiae, cited for alchemy's antiquity, the Lully gold-coin story, transmutation stories and a count of 2500 authors.
E1213.body: Atwood cites his *De Ortu et Progressu Chemiae* in support of alchemy's antiquity, calling him “the learned Dane” [I.1 ¶3, I.1 n3]; for the story of Lully and the English gold coins: “Aureas illas Anglorum primum...” [I.1 ¶47, I.1 n57]; and (as Borricius) for counting 2500 authors and for transmutation stories [I.1 ¶75, I.1 n96, I.1 n104].

E1214.summary: Traditional maxims Atwood cites in the Appendix on the transmission of spirit and the wisdom of the receiver.
E1214.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood cites “Ut ventus qui flat, est ille qui dat” [APP ¶41] (ours: as the wind that blows, so is he who gives) for the imparter of spirit as wind, and “Qui capit, ille sapit” (ours: he who receives, he is wise) for the wisdom of the receiver [APP ¶41].

E1215.summary: Collective authority whose definition of the Matter Atwood endorses: bodies are to be turned into vapour, which is the Stone.
E1215.body: Atwood cites and endorses the old Alchemists' definition of the Matter: “it is no common water, but an unctuous mineral vapour, universally subsisting” [III.2 ¶7]; bodies are to be turned into vapour, and this is the Stone [III.2 ¶7].

E1216.summary: A mythic analogy Atwood uses in the Appendix to illustrate drawing the Salt up into the medial life.
E1216.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Troy in the old analogy is that citadel where Apollo keeps his cattle” [APP ¶77], used to illustrate drawing the Salt up into the medial life; how the image maps onto the operation is not spelled out in the record.

E1217.summary: Scripture, cited in the Appendix as founded on revealed utterance, with the New fulfilling the Old's promise and giving another.
E1217.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood illustrates with the Testaments: both are founded on the revealed utterance; the New fulfils the Old's promise and gives another [APP ¶98].

E1218.summary: Authority cited (lib. Concilio, Quest 74) as having praised the Hermetic Art and Arnold's wisdom.
E1218.body: Cited in support: he praised the Hermetic Art and Arnold's wisdom [I.1 ¶43, I.1 n52].

E1219.summary: In Khunrath's words, a fire with which the internal and external fire must be in sympathy; the text does not define it.
E1219.body: Voice: QUOTED: Khunrath. The internal and external fire must be “in harmonious sympathy with the Olympic Fire” [III.3 ¶9]. The passage does not say what the Olympic Fire is.

E1220.summary: 'The Egyptian Olympiodorus', cited in support on phantasy as an impediment, allegorical readings of Elysium and Tartarus, and reason's rule over the soul.
E1220.body: Atwood cites him approvingly. Phantasy opposes divine enthusiasm, and perceiving Universals proves the soul can act without it: “The phantasy, says he, is an impediment to our intellectual conception” [II.2 ¶12, II.2 n13]. From his Commentary on the Gorgias she takes an allegorical reading of Hercules' last labour and of the Islands of the Blessed / Elysian Fields as a state above corporeal life: “islands stand out of, as being higher than the sea” [II.4 ¶3]. He also supports an ethical/physical reading of Tartarus: “souls, in which reason does not preside as a charioteer, are changed according to the subject temperament of the body” [III.2 ¶9, III.2 n11]. He is listed among authors of extant treatises on the philosophers’ stone [I.1 ¶27, I.1 n34].

E1221.summary: The philosophers' absolute unit, Fountain of all being, implied in every multitude and each part; reported from Xenophanes as God.
E1221.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) says “the One of these philosophers is the Fountain of all being” [III.2 ¶45], implied in every multitude and each part; “if any one should undertake to demonstrate the philosopher’s Unit, he would unfold Being” [III.2 ¶45]. She also reports Xenophanes, via Aristotle (QUOTED), identifying it with God: “looking to the whole heaven, he says, the One is God” [III.2 ¶40].

E1222.summary: In Agrippa's words, the single thing besides which there is no other, the subject of the most holy stone, of which to speak rashly is sacrilege.
E1222.body: Voice: QUOTED: Cornelius Agrippa. He speaks “of the one blessed stone alone, besides which there is no other thing, the subject of the most holy stone of the philosophers” [I.1 ¶64], treating rash speech of it as sacrilege [I.1 ¶64].

E1223.summary: The ancient theory of a single vitalizing principle in air and all things, which Atwood says moderns deride because it escapes their analyses.
E1223.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) notes that “the ancient theory of the One Element has been very much derided” [I.2 ¶14], because the single vitalizing principle in air and all things escapes modern analyses [I.2 ¶14]; her tone implies she does not share the derision.

E1224.summary: The single matter of all things in the Beginning, which the process imitates as all diversities come from and return to the One.
E1224.body: Atwood (ATWOOD): “as in the Beginning there was said to be one only matter of all things” [III.3 ¶29], so in the process all diversities proceed from and return to the One [III.3 ¶29].

E1225.summary: In Proclus' words, the principle found only by becoming assimilated to it, the most united in nature, uniting the universe in sympathetic consent.
E1225.body: Voice: QUOTED: Proclus. “if any one wish to discover the One Principle he must become first assimilated to it” [III.2 ¶50]. It is the most united in nature, through which it is Deity, uniting the universe in sympathetic consent [III.2 ¶50].
